analysis.one_liner: Requires nursing homes to reveal their owners, publish real staffing data, and face stronger enforcement.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Finance Committee, and no version of it ever received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required nursing homes to publicly disclose the companies and individuals who own and profit from them—an answer to the common setup where the real estate and management are split off from the facility to shield parent companies from liability. It would also have put verifiable staffing and spending data on the government's nursing home comparison website, created a standard complaint process for residents, forced 60 days' notice and relocation planning before a home closes, added ethics and quality programs for large chains, and tightened penalties for violations. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action.
analysis.who_benefits: Nursing home residents and their families gain the biggest share: clearer ownership information, honest staffing data, a workable complaint system, and protection when a facility shuts down. Taxpayers who fund more than $75 billion a year in Medicare and Medicaid nursing home payments would gain visibility into where that money actually goes [S3]. Direct care workers benefit from disclosure of wage and staffing practices.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Nursing home residents, families, and taxpayers

how_it_helps.text: Requires nursing homes to disclose who actually owns and controls them—including parent companies, lenders, landlords, and management firms—so regulators and the public can hold the real operators accountable.

Improves the federal Nursing Home Compare website with auditable payroll-based staffing data, turnover rates, inspection links, complaint and enforcement histories, and wage/benefit spending on direct care staff.
Creates a standardized complaint form and requires states to run complaint resolution processes with deadlines and anti-retaliation protections.
Requires administrators to give 60 days' notice before a facility closes, with an approved plan to relocate every resident safely.

Establishes a quality assurance and performance improvement program, an independent monitor pilot for poorly performing chains, dementia and abuse-prevention training for aides, and rules governing civil monetary penalties—including escrowed penalty funds used to relocate residents from closing facilities.

analysis.who_pays: Nursing home operators and corporate chains would bear compliance costs: disclosure of ownership and financial relationships, compliance and ethics programs, auditable payroll-based staffing reports, separate wage/benefit reporting, independent monitor costs for problem chains, and revised penalty rules. Taxpayers would fund the new studies, pilot programs, and demonstrations.
analysis.who_pays_short: Nursing home owners and corporate chains

drawbacks.text: Facilities that self-report and fix a violation within 10 days could see penalties cut by up to half, a concession the bill makes to providers that critics could argue weakens enforcement.

Most of the bill's force depends on HHS writing regulations—ownership disclosure rules, staffing reporting, quality standards—which means a slow or friendly administration could gut its effect without Congress acting.
Compliance and ethics programs, standardized payroll reporting, and independent monitors add reporting and administrative costs for nursing home operators, especially small facilities.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are real but modest by design: disclosure, posted staffing data, complaint forms, and closure notices cost little and would directly help families choosing care and residents facing a closing home. The costs fall on the industry—compliance programs, verifiable staffing reporting, corporate transparency, and some penalty payments redirected to residents. Supporters would concede the bill relies on regulators to use the new information, and its penalty "improvements" include a self-report discount that could soften enforcement in ordinary cases. The bigger weakness is that it was never even debated, so none of its merits were ever tested.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it, so it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Grassley introduced the bill with Senator Herb Kohl on March 19, 2009, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day.
No further action was ever recorded—no hearings, no markup, no floor vote—before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

The bill's findings state that CMS pays nursing homes more than $75 billion a year without always knowing who the owners and operators are, and that separating real estate from operations can frustrate efforts to hold parent companies accountable for care quality.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nursing home owners and chains keep their current ability to obscure ownership and face no new disclosure, staffing, or penalty requirements.

for.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
for.role: U.S. Senator (R-IA), senior member of the Senate Finance Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and served as its lead sponsor.

for.name: Sen. Herb Kohl
for.role: U.S. Senator (D-WI), chairman of the Senate Aging Committee

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Never took up the bill—no hearings, markup, or vote are recorded in its action history after the referral.

against.name: Nursing home industry
against.role: Providers and corporate chains affected by the bill
against.what_they_did: Opposed transparency and enforcement legislation of this kind, lobbying against provisions that would expose corporate ownership structures and increase penalties.

sides.party_line_note: A senior Republican introduced the bill and three Senate Democrats cosponsored it, so support was bipartisan; the record shows no recorded opposition, only inaction in committee.

industries.industry: Nursing home operators and chains (skilled nursing and nursing facilities)
industries.note: The bill requires corporate ownership disclosure, auditable payroll-based staffing reporting, compliance programs, a national independent monitor pilot for bad chains, 60-day closure notices, and penalty rules. It removes the ability to hide behind layered ownership when regulators pursue quality violations.

industries.industry: Nursing home landlords, lenders, and management/consulting firms
industries.note: These entities would become 'additional disclosable parties' required to be identified publicly, ending the common practice of separating real estate from operations to shield owners from accountability. The bill targets exactly this structure.

industries.industry: Nursing home residents and their families
industries.note: Residents and families gain transparency on staffing and enforcement, a real complaint process, and protection from sudden closures. This is a beneficiary group rather than an industry, but it is the core stakeholder.

Payroll-based staffing and wage/benefit reporting would expose understaffing and pay practices, pressure that could improve working conditions; dementia and abuse-prevention training requirements add to staff duties. The bill never passed, so no effect occurred.
